children.title: Track Hopper Feeder Start, Stop & Inspection under Supervision
children.content: You have completed L1 — you know what the system is and why it matters. This course prepares you for the next stage: assisted execution . You will work alongside a supervisor, observe, support, and learn to read what the system is telling you. Skill 1 Assist in Starting and Stopping Feeder Skill 2 Assist in Inspecting Coal at Feeder Input Mode Supervised execution only Pre-req L1 Wagon Tippler completed

children.title: The Track Hopper Feeder — A Quick Refresh
children.content: You learned in L1 that coal discharged from the Wagon Tippler falls into the Underground Hopper. The Track Hopper Feeder is the device that meters coal from the bottom of that hopper onto the downstream belt conveyor at a controlled, steady rate. There are two main types you will encounter in Indian thermal power plants: WAGON tippled HOPPER FEEDER ★ THIS COURSE BELT CONVEYOR CRUSHER HOUSE COAL BUNKER / STOCK MILL → BOILER GENERATION POSITION OF FEEDER IN COAL FLOW CHAIN Every tonne through the boiler passes through this feeder first

children.title: Two Feeder Types You Will Encounter
children.content: Uses electromagnetic or mechanical vibration to move coal along a trough. Simpler design, lower maintenance, well-suited to fine coal. Flow rate is adjusted by changing vibration amplitude or frequency. Common at: smaller CHP installations, older plants Uses a slow-moving steel apron or rubber belt to carry coal from the hopper outlet. Handles larger lumps and heavier material well. Flow rate controlled by feeder speed and a slide gate above. Common at: large-capacity plants, high-throughput systems

children.title: Execution Block 1: Feeder Start Sequence
What Happens When the Feeder Starts
children.content: 0 FEEDER START CMD supervisor initiates ~5s MOTOR ACCELERATES observe sound/vibration ~15s FIRST COAL HITS BELT observation window opens ~1min STEADY STATE FLOW confirm normal operation cont. PERIODIC MONITORING rounds every shift
children.parent_title: Execution Block 1: Feeder Start Sequence

children.title: Control Point 1 — Pre-Start System Readiness Check
children.content: The downstream belt conveyor must be confirmed running and at the correct speed before feeder start is commanded. This confirmation comes from the control room or from the supervisor who has checked belt status on the SCADA/PLC system. As a trainee, you do not have the authority or system access to confirm belt status — this is a supervisor action. Your role: Stand at the feeder local panel area, observe the feeder visually, and listen for the supervisor's instruction to proceed. Do not touch the start pushbutton unless specifically directed. Before start, the hopper should have sufficient coal to sustain initial flow. You can assist by checking the hopper level indicator (if visible locally) or reading the level gauge and reporting the reading to your supervisor. Low hopper level may cause intermittent feeding — important to note before starting. What to report: Hopper level reading. Presence of any blockage at the hopper throat. Any unusual odours or visible smoke from the hopper area (can indicate spontaneous combustion). Confirm that no personnel are in the feeder zone — under the feeder trough, near the discharge end, or inside the underground hopper area. Both you and your supervisor walk the immediate zone before any start command is issued. This is a procedural safety step and is never skipped regardless of time pressure.
children.parent_title: Execution Block 1: Feeder Start Sequence

children.title: Control Point 2 — Initial Coal Flow Observation Window
children.content: Coal begins flowing steadily from the feeder outlet — no surging, no sudden large lumps, no gaps in flow OBSERVE Feeder drive motor sound is smooth and consistent — no grinding, banging, or cyclical thumping LISTEN Coal falls centrally on the belt at the transfer point — not to one side (which causes belt mis-tracking) OBSERVE No unusual coal dust cloud beyond normal — excessive dust at startup indicates high coal velocity or faulty dust suppression OBSERVE Feeder ampere reading (motor current) is within normal range — supervisor confirms on SCADA; high current at startup can indicate blockage or material jam SUPERVISOR Belt load cell / weigh feeder reading is increasing normally — supervisor confirms material is being placed on belt as expected SUPERVISOR

children.title: Control Point 3 — Assisted Stop Under Live Load
children.content: Supervisor confirms downstream belt will continue running for the clearing period after feeder stop — this is non-negotiable SUPERVISOR You observe the feeder discharge end — watch for the coal tail-off: flow should reduce progressively, not cut off with a sudden material surge OBSERVE Watch the transfer point on the belt — coal should spread evenly during tail-off, not pile up on one edge OBSERVE Feeder motor sound should reduce smoothly to silence — an abnormal grinding or metallic sound during deceleration is a warning sign to report immediately LISTEN Hopper throat gate closure (if applicable) — commanded by supervisor before or at stop to limit residual flow SUPERVISOR After motor stops: both trainee and supervisor confirm the feeder is stationary before anyone approaches the feeder for inspection JOINT

children.title: Observation Windows — Reading System Behaviour
children.content: A large part of your value as an L2 learner is your presence on the floor . Instruments are not everywhere, and local observation is a genuine layer of protection. Knowing what normal looks like is the only way to recognise abnormal.

children.title: Normal vs. Abnormal — Quick Reference
children.content: What You Are Watching | Normal Condition | Early Warning | Act ; Coal flow from feeder outlet | Steady, continuous, even width | Pulsing, gaps, surges | REPORT ; Coal landing on belt | Centred, consistent pile height | Displaced to one side | REPORT ; Feeder motor sound | Smooth, consistent hum | Thumping, grinding, cyclical sound | REPORT IMMEDIATELY ; Feeder trough vibration | Even vibration (vibratory type) or smooth movement (apron type) | Irregular, jerky, or hammering vibration | REPORT ; Dust levels at feeder | Low; water mist visible from suppression | Dust cloud increasing; mist absent | REPORT ; Coal smell | Normal fresh coal odour | Burning or acrid smell | REPORT IMMEDIATELY ; Motor casing temperature | Warm to back of hand — not hot | Hot — cannot hold hand near casing | REPORT IMMEDIATELY ; Belt tracking at transfer point | Belt running centrally on idlers | Belt drifting to one side | REPORT ; Hopper throat area | Open, coal freely moving downward | Coal bridging / arch forming | REPORT IMMEDIATELY
children.parent_title: Observation Windows — Reading System Behaviour

children.title: Common Mistakes in Assisted Execution
children.content: These are the execution errors that occur most often among trainees during their first supervised interactions with feeder systems. They are not listed to make you nervous — they are listed so you recognise the pattern if you start heading toward it. Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Severity ; Touching the start button before supervisor confirms system readiness | Eagerness to help; mistaking presence of button for permission to use it | Feeder starts before downstream belt is ready; spillage or belt trip | HIGH ; Standing in the coal discharge fall zone during observation | Wanting a better viewing angle; not knowing the designated safe observation point | Coal impact injury; coal dust inhalation; being caught in moving material | HIGH ; Treating inspection as a quick visual pass — not pausing to observe carefully | Time pressure; assumption that nothing will be wrong | Hazardous material (tramp iron, oversized coal) enters the system undetected | HIGH ; Not reporting an early warning condition because "it seems minor" | Self-doubt; not wanting to raise a false alarm; not knowing what normal is | Small issues become failures; early warning missed means later incident | HIGH ; Walking away from the feeder during the post-start observation window | Feeling that once it starts, the job is done | Abnormal behaviour in the first 60 seconds goes undetected | MEDIUM ; Not accounting for inertia during a stop — assuming coal stops when the motor stops | Intuition from everyday experience (switches turn things off instantly) | Misreads the discharge end as clear when coal is still flowing; wrong report | MEDIUM ; Attempting to remove obstruction from the feeder trough | Wanting to solve the problem; not wanting to slow things down | Entanglement injury; crush injury; falls into trough | CRITICAL / FATAL

children.title: Risk Summary — Three Dimensions
children.content: Risk Dimension | Trigger Scenario | Potential Consequence | Severity ; Plant Continuity | Feeder trip during peak coal demand; blockage of hopper throat; belt damage from mis-tracking | Downstream conveyor starvation → bunker depletion → mill trip → unit derate. In a tight coal stock situation, even a 2-hour feeder outage can force load reduction. | HIGH ; Machinery Integrity | Tramp iron through feeder; oversized lump blocking apron chain; uncontrolled start/stop loading belt | Feeder chain/pan damage requiring replacement; belt edge damage from mis-tracking; crusher tooth breakage from oversized material. Repair downtime: hours to days. | HIGH ; Human Safety | Approach to running feeder zone without clearance; attempt to clear blockage manually; entry into hopper area without LOTO; ignoring burning smell | Entanglement in moving feeder mechanism; coal burial in hopper; burn injury from spontaneous combustion; respiratory injury from coal dust. Consequences are potentially fatal. | CRITICAL

textchunk_objects.content: Two Feeder Types You Will Encounter Uses electromagnetic or mechanical vibration to move coal along a trough. Simpler design, lower maintenance, well-suited to fine coal. Flow rate is adjusted by changing vibration amplitude or frequency. Common at: smaller CHP installations, older plants Uses a slow-moving steel apron or rubber belt to carry coal from the hopper outlet. Handles larger lumps and heavier material well. Flow rate controlled by feeder speed and a slide gate above. Common at: large-capacity plants, high-throughput systems

What Happens When the Feeder Starts

textchunk_objects.content: Control Point 1 — Pre-Start System Readiness Check The downstream belt conveyor must be confirmed running and at the correct speed before feeder start is commanded. This confirmation comes from the control room or from the supervisor who has checked belt status on the SCADA/PLC system. As a trainee, you do not have the authority or system access to confirm belt status — this is a supervisor action. Your role: Stand at the feeder local panel area, observe the feeder visually, and listen for the supervisor's instruction to proceed. Do not touch the start pushbutton unless specifically directed. Before start, the hopper should have sufficient coal to sustain initial flow. You can assist by checking the hopper level indicator (if visible locally) or reading the level gauge and reporting the reading to your supervisor. Low hopper level may cause intermittent feeding — important to note before starting. What to report: Hopper level reading. Presence of any blockage at the hopper throat. Any unusual odours or visible smoke from the hopper area (can indicate spontaneous combustion). Confirm that no personnel are in the feeder zone — under the feeder trough, near the discharge end, or inside the underground hopper area. Both you and your supervisor walk the immediate zone before any start command is issued. This is a procedural safety step and is never skipped regardless of time pressure.

textchunk_objects.content: Control Point 2 — Initial Coal Flow Observation Window Coal begins flowing steadily from the feeder outlet — no surging, no sudden large lumps, no gaps in flow OBSERVE Feeder drive motor sound is smooth and consistent — no grinding, banging, or cyclical thumping LISTEN Coal falls centrally on the belt at the transfer point — not to one side (which causes belt mis-tracking) OBSERVE No unusual coal dust cloud beyond normal — excessive dust at startup indicates high coal velocity or faulty dust suppression OBSERVE Feeder ampere reading (motor current) is within normal range — supervisor confirms on SCADA; high current at startup can indicate blockage or material jam SUPERVISOR Belt load cell / weigh feeder reading is increasing normally — supervisor confirms material is being placed on belt as expected SUPERVISOR

textchunk_objects.content: Control Point 3 — Assisted Stop Under Live Load Supervisor confirms downstream belt will continue running for the clearing period after feeder stop — this is non-negotiable SUPERVISOR You observe the feeder discharge end — watch for the coal tail-off: flow should reduce progressively, not cut off with a sudden material surge OBSERVE Watch the transfer point on the belt — coal should spread evenly during tail-off, not pile up on one edge OBSERVE Feeder motor sound should reduce smoothly to silence — an abnormal grinding or metallic sound during deceleration is a warning sign to report immediately LISTEN Hopper throat gate closure (if applicable) — commanded by supervisor before or at stop to limit residual flow SUPERVISOR After motor stops: both trainee and supervisor confirm the feeder is stationary before anyone approaches the feeder for inspection JOINT

textchunk_objects.content: Observation Windows — Reading System Behaviour A large part of your value as an L2 learner is your presence on the floor . Instruments are not everywhere, and local observation is a genuine layer of protection. Knowing what normal looks like is the only way to recognise abnormal.

textchunk_objects.content: Normal vs. Abnormal — Quick Reference What You Are Watching | Normal Condition | Early Warning | Act ; Coal flow from feeder outlet | Steady, continuous, even width | Pulsing, gaps, surges | REPORT ; Coal landing on belt | Centred, consistent pile height | Displaced to one side | REPORT ; Feeder motor sound | Smooth, consistent hum | Thumping, grinding, cyclical sound | REPORT IMMEDIATELY ; Feeder trough vibration | Even vibration (vibratory type) or smooth movement (apron type) | Irregular, jerky, or hammering vibration | REPORT ; Dust levels at feeder | Low; water mist visible from suppression | Dust cloud increasing; mist absent | REPORT ; Coal smell | Normal fresh coal odour | Burning or acrid smell | REPORT IMMEDIATELY ; Motor casing temperature | Warm to back of hand — not hot | Hot — cannot hold hand near casing | REPORT IMMEDIATELY ; Belt tracking at transfer point | Belt running centrally on idlers | Belt drifting to one side | REPORT ; Hopper throat area | Open, coal freely moving downward | Coal bridging / arch forming | REPORT IMMEDIATELY

textchunk_objects.content: Common Mistakes in Assisted Execution These are the execution errors that occur most often among trainees during their first supervised interactions with feeder systems. They are not listed to make you nervous — they are listed so you recognise the pattern if you start heading toward it. Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Severity ; Touching the start button before supervisor confirms system readiness | Eagerness to help; mistaking presence of button for permission to use it | Feeder starts before downstream belt is ready; spillage or belt trip | HIGH ; Standing in the coal discharge fall zone during observation | Wanting a better viewing angle; not knowing the designated safe observation point | Coal impact injury; coal dust inhalation; being caught in moving material | HIGH ; Treating inspection as a quick visual pass — not pausing to observe carefully | Time pressure; assumption that nothing will be wrong | Hazardous material (tramp iron, oversized coal) enters the system undetected | HIGH ; Not reporting an early warning condition because "it seems minor" | Self-doubt; not wanting to raise a false alarm; not knowing what normal is | Small issues become failures; early warning missed means later incident | HIGH ; Walking away from the feeder during the post-start observation window | Feeling that once it starts, the job is done | Abnormal behaviour in the first 60 seconds goes undetected | MEDIUM ; Not accounting for inertia during a stop — assuming coal stops when the motor stops | Intuition from everyday experience (switches turn things off instantly) | Misreads the discharge end as clear when coal is still flowing; wrong report | MEDIUM ; Attempting to remove obstruction from the feeder trough | Wanting to solve the problem; not wanting to slow things down | Entanglement injury; crush injury; falls into trough | CRITICAL / FATAL

textchunk_objects.content: Risk Summary — Three Dimensions Risk Dimension | Trigger Scenario | Potential Consequence | Severity ; Plant Continuity | Feeder trip during peak coal demand; blockage of hopper throat; belt damage from mis-tracking | Downstream conveyor starvation → bunker depletion → mill trip → unit derate. In a tight coal stock situation, even a 2-hour feeder outage can force load reduction. | HIGH ; Machinery Integrity | Tramp iron through feeder; oversized lump blocking apron chain; uncontrolled start/stop loading belt | Feeder chain/pan damage requiring replacement; belt edge damage from mis-tracking; crusher tooth breakage from oversized material. Repair downtime: hours to days. | HIGH ; Human Safety | Approach to running feeder zone without clearance; attempt to clear blockage manually; entry into hopper area without LOTO; ignoring burning smell | Entanglement in moving feeder mechanism; coal burial in hopper; burn injury from spontaneous combustion; respiratory injury from coal dust. Consequences are potentially fatal. | CRITICAL
